stop_condition: Every acceptance criterion in the SPEC is discharged by measurement rather than by reading: the shim fix independently reproduced against a hand-built mutant proven byte-identical to the true pre-fix shim, the scoping claims (cpid grouping, 13.A/13.G cap-fires, grandchild reap) verified by direct pgid observation, the bash 3.2 empty-array claim executed on this host, and no claim left standing that nothing checks. Stop when no finding at or above high remains unrecorded.

findings.location: .claude/scripts/tests/green-check.test.sh:1187-1284 (13.B-TEARDOWN, 13.B-TEARDOWN-META.5, the cleanup loop between META.5 and META.6, and 13.B-TEARDOWN-META.7)
findings.evidence: THE LOAD-BEARING PREMISE IS FALSE AND I MEASURED IT. The comment at :1195-1199 justifies an unowned global selector by asserting that dur=20 is 'far enough from every OTHER duration this file ever uses (6.*, 60, 600, 8, 3, 1) that a bare, unadorned `sleep 20` cannot be confused with anything else'. That enumeration omits 20, which THIS SAME FILE uses at :594 -- `set_test_cmd "sleep 20; echo should-not-finish"` (Section 10.1). I ran that exact command and read the process table with 13.B-TEARDOWN's own awk: it yields `57881 57879 57873 sleep 20` -- $4=="sleep", $5=="20", NF==5, a byte-exact match, and GC13B_TEARDOWN_LEAKED computes to 1 where the assertion demands 0. I then sampled the process table once a second through a full shipped run of the spec (rc=0, 144/144, 84s): a bare `sleep 20` was live on the host at t=26 and t=27 (`59138 59135 59135 sleep 20`, ppid a process-group leader == qa-gate.sh's WATCHDOG `set -m` bracket, visible for exactly the 2s cap), and again at t=52 (`60135 1 58074 sleep 20`, the mutant's own orphan). Two distinct producers of the same needle inside one run. THREE CONSEQUENCES, ONE ROOT. (a) META.5 is the SPECIFIC-MISBEHAVIOUR leg and carries the entire non-vacuity claim; it asserts count>0, which ANY bare `sleep 20` on the host satisfies, so it can pass without the mutant having leaked anything. (b) The cleanup loop `for _meta_td_pid in $MUTANT_LEAKED_PIDS; do kill -9` then kills every globally-matched pid, owned or not -- it LAUNDERS the contamination, so META.7 samples a clean table and also passes: the pair goes GREEN having proved nothing, and it kills a host process it does not own. (c) 13.B-TEARDOWN's assertion name blames the shim for any bare `sleep 20` anywhere on the machine. REACHABILITY IS NOT SPECULATIVE AND IS THIS FILE'S OWN HISTORY. Section 10.1's sleep is reaped today only because qa-gate.sh's WATCHDOG tree-kill works; docs/reviews/claude-workflow-plugin-fkm.7-r6.json R6-F1 already established (i) that this exact bare `sleep 20` leaf is what leaks when that tree-kill regresses and (ii) that Section 10.3's own instrument `pgrep -f "sleep 20; echo should-not-finish"` is BLIND to it (0 hits against the orphan). So ONE regression, in a different file, puts the needle on the host inside this spec's own window. Timing, measured not assumed: locally 10.1 fires at t~25 and 13.B-TEARDOWN samples at t~50, so an unreaped 20s sleep expires at t~45 -- a 5-second margin on an 84-second run, which is luck rather than design. CI runs this same spec in 37-40s; the compressible work shrinks ~3x while the 20s sleep does not compress at all, putting 10.1 at t~9-11 and 13.B-TEARDOWN/META.5 at t~21-23, i.e. INSIDE the leak's lifetime. The collision is reachable on the exact platform this fix exists to serve.
findings.description: The new check and its mutation pair select processes by an unowned global predicate in a file whose own review history spent four rounds making selection ownership-proving, and the comment that authorises the choice is falsified by the same file 600 lines up. The repair is the one R6-F1 already prescribed for this file: put the uniqueness in the DURATION. Give 13.B (and its META legs) a cap no other producer uses -- GREEN_CHECK_TIMEOUT_S=2011 -- so the shim's internal timer is `sleep 2011` and the needle is unmistakable; the 'nowhere near the cap' semantics 13.B tests are indifferent to the exact value. Alternatively snapshot the matching pid set BEFORE the invocation and assert/kill only on the delta. DO NOT repair this with a pgid filter: I checked, and it would be WRONG -- after this fix the killer subshell sits in its OWN process group, so a future regression that kept `set -m` but dropped the group-kill would be invisible to a pgid-scoped scan. The global scan is the right instrument; it needs a unique needle, not a narrower scope. Whichever repair is chosen, the kill loop must never signal a pid the spec cannot prove it owns.

findings.location: .claude/scripts/tests/green-check.test.sh:100-119 and :154-177 (GC13_BYSTANDER_PIDS and the extended cleanup() EXIT trap)
findings.evidence: THE CLAIM IS TRUE AND NOTHING IN THE REPO CHECKS IT -- I had to build the check myself to find that out. The file states at :1069 'Residual risk, named in round 7, CLOSED in claude-workflow-plugin-tnue' and the commit message states it 'closes the residual risk round 9 documented and accepted'. I extracted the shipped declaration, cleanup() body and trap registration verbatim and drove four scenarios: (1) empty array, normal exit -> rc=0, no unbound-variable abort, so the length guard holds; (2) abort BEFORE registration (the pre-fix world, the negative control) -> both bystanders still alive after exit, so the residual risk was real; (3) abort AFTER registration via a `set -u` unbound variable -> rc=1 and all three bystanders reaped, including the deliberately foreign-pgid one; (4) external SIGTERM mid-run -> reaped. The mechanism works. But no assertion in the shipped spec, and no other spec in the repo, exercises any of it; .claude/tests/README.md 'The pairing requirement' makes this a closeout obligation -- 'every check added by the change is either paired to the standard below or listed as UNPAIRED with a reason' -- and it is neither. I also confirmed the two structural preconditions the comment relies on: the declaration at :119 precedes the trap registration at :177 so the trap can never fire against an undeclared array, and registration coverage is COMPLETE (all nine directly-backgrounded bystanders at :1022-1024, :1082-1083, :1117-1118, :1153-1154 are registered; the only other `&` lines in the file, :274 and :283, are inside the shim heredoc and are a different process).
findings.description: A risk-closing mechanism whose closure claim rests entirely on reading. It is trivially testable at L1 -- the probe that convinced me is about forty lines and drives the shipped bytes directly -- so the stronger of the two options the pairing requirement offers is available: pair it (spawn a bystander, register it, abort, assert the process is gone; negative control = the same scenario with the registration removed, which I already measured leaking). If it is not paired, it must be declared UNPAIRED with a reason, per the same section.

findings.location: .claude/scripts/tests/green-check.test.sh:165-170 (the cleanup() kill loop) with the registrations at :1029, :1084, :1119, :1155
findings.evidence: The array accumulates nine pids, every one of which its own block already kills inline within ~0.3s of capture, and then `kill -9`s all nine again at EXIT with no liveness or identity check. Measured on this host during the shipped run: the registrations land around t~25-30 and cleanup fires at t~84, and the pid counter advanced from 59138 to 60135 across 26 seconds of that window (~1000 pids per 26s, so roughly 2500 pids elapse between capture and the trap). In the normal path every one of those nine kills is a no-op against a dead pid and buys nothing; the mechanism's only value is the abort path. A recycled pid would be signalled by identity-free reference. The comment at :112-118 defends the bare-pid form on the grounds that it reaches foreign process groups -- which is correct and which I verified -- but it never addresses identity.
findings.description: Bounded and unlikely to fire within one spec (2500 pids is far from any pid_max wrap), and I am not asking for it to block. Recording it because this is the one file in the repo that spent four review rounds establishing that a teardown must prove what it owns, and a stale pid list is the same class of reference with the proof removed. A `kill -0` liveness gate before each kill, or capturing a start-time/argv witness alongside the pid, would close it for a line or two.
